Box 9020 Monrovia, Liberia 2 Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA Author to whom correspondence should be addressed. † These authors contributed equally to the study. Submission received: 24 July 2018 / Revised: 11 August 2018 / Accepted: 13 August 2018 / Published: 15 August 2018 Abstract It is well documented that flotation has high economic viability for the beneficiation of valuable minerals when their main ore bodies contain magnesium (Mg) carbonates such as dolomite and magnesite. Flotation separation of Mg carbonates from their associated valuable minerals (AVMs) presents several challenges, and Mg carbonates have high levels of adverse effects on separation efficiency. These complexities can be attributed to various reasons: Mg carbonates are naturally hydrophilic, soluble, and exhibit similar surface characteristics as their AVMs. This study presents a compilation of various parameters, including zeta potential, pH, particle size, reagents (collectors, depressant, and modifiers), and bio-flotation, which were examined in several investigations into separating Mg carbonates from their AVMs by froth flotation. 1. Introduction Magnesium (Mg) carbonates (salt-type minerals) are typical gangue phases associated with several valuable minerals, and have complicated processing [1,2]. Dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2) and magnesite (MgCO3) are the main Mg carbonates [3,4,5,6,7,8] that can be associated with other salt-type minerals, including phosphates (e.g., Apatite), sulfates (e.g., Barite), halides (e.g., Fluorite) and tungstates (e.g., Scheelite) [5,9], as well as sulfides [10], and other oxides [2]. The ease of separation of Mg carbonates from their associated valuable minerals (AVMs) is dependent on various processing conditions. To achieve adequate separation efficiency, different processing methods based on AVM properties have been used: magnetic separation [8], dense medium separation [1,8,11,12,13], electronic sorting techniques (when iron and titanium oxides are AVMs) [1,8], calcination [8,11] and froth flotation [1,8,10,11,13,14,15]. The first flotation separation for the rejection of magnesite was reported by Doerner and Dwigh (1930s) [12]. Flotation of Mg carbonates is typically carried out by using fatty acids, since these collectors give insoluble complexes with all divalent cations [5]. Determination of the appropriate depressing reagents for sinking valuable minerals in the presence of collectors for carbonates is a cardinal stage in obtaining an efficient separation in the direct flotation of Mg carbonate [7]. One of the essential challenges during flotation in the presence of Mg carbonate is the occurrence of slimes. The low hardness of carbonates leads to slime problems. Carbonate slimes can cover the surfaces of their AVMs, change their properties, and make their flotation complicated [11,16,17,18]. Moreover, Mg carbonates are semi-soluble and hydrophilic in nature; the dissolved species of carbonates undergo reactions such as hydrolysis, complexation, adsorption, and bulk precipitations, which inhibit the selective interaction of flotation reagents with surfaces of minerals [2,12,19,20,21,22]. Therefore, rejection of Mg carbonates prior to processing of other minerals has been recommended. Nevertheless, even with these rejections, selectivity is still a major challenge in achieving satisfactory separation [6,11], especially when the valuable mineral is also a salt-type mineral, and complexity increases [5,6,23] due to the similarities in crystal structure (crystalline and sedimentary minerals behave similarly, but the crystalline minerals have much lower surface areas and consume less collector than the sedimentary minerals) and physiochemical surface properties [17,18,24,25]. Thus, a literature review for flotation of Mg carbonates could be useful and suggest new directions for future investigations. The aim of this paper is to provide a robust review of various flotation conditions for Mg carbonates, with a focus on the collectors, depressant, modifiers, isoelectric point, particle size, and solubility of these minerals during flotation. 2. Particle Size Effect Particle size and degree of mineral liberation are important factors for flotation separation [26]. Grinding of salt-type minerals to liberate them is quite challenging where their solubility is increased by reducing their sizes (ions of salt minerals in the pulp undergo various hydrolysis reactions, forming different complexes) [15]. It has been reported that coarse particles of Mg carbonates are relatively able to float, and separation of fine particles by flotation would have several difficulties [27]. Fine dolomite particles can cover the surface of other AVMs and change their surface properties [23]. Xi-mei et al. [2] reported that during the beneficiation of hematite, fine dolomites (−45 + 18 µm) significantly affected the final concentrate recovery. Fine carbonates (−45 µm) exhibit low selectivity in flotation systems [23]; floating these fines would require an immense increase in the collector concentration beyond economic viability. Furthermore, the entrainment effect of fine carbonates can significantly increase the losses of valuable minerals in the froth (reverse flotation) [22,28,29,30]. In general, coarse particle size favors the selective separation of Mg carbonates from oxides, while decreasing the particle size could be complicated for their separation from other salt-type minerals. fetched_contents.text: Enhancing selectivity of modifier on magnesite and dolomite surfaces by pH control Introduction Magnesite is the most important raw material utilized in the refrac-tories industry for the manufacturing of basic refractories, having ahigh corrosion resistance in the presence of basic slags, dusts and fumes [1]. The reserves of magnesite in China are 13 billion tons, taking the first place in the world [2]. However, with the development of industry and increase in demand, high-grade magnesite is gradually exhausting, and the use of low-grade magnesite is being studied. Owing to its formation characteristic, magnesite coexists with carbonate minerals and other gangue minerals, and magnesite deposits with dolomite gangue are known [[3], [4], [5]]. Effective flotation separation of magnesite and dolomite is found to be difficult owing to the similarity in their crystal structure, chemical composition, and dispulp behavior [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. It has been reported that owing to the dispulp equilibrium of calcium ions from the surface of dolomite, the calcium precipitated on the surface of magnesite can decrease the selectivity of the reagents for the flotation separation of magnesite and dolomite. This can make the flotation more difficult [9]. In the flotation of single minerals with sodium carbonate and sodium hexametaphosphate (SH) as the modifier and sodium oleate (NaOL) as the collector, a difference in the recovery of both the minerals was observed; however, the selective separation efficiency of the modifier was not significant for the mixed minerals. Based on the observation, it was found that the species of calcium that dissolved from dolomite were adsorbed on the surface of magnesite, which resulted in the similarity of their subsequent adsorption behavior for sodium oleate and surface composition. There exists previous research investigating effective flotation separation of both the minerals using several reagents. In the flotation tests with N-dodecyl-isopropanolamine (DIPA) [10], NaOL [11], mixtures of NaOL and monohydric alcohols [12], and mixtures of dodecylamine (DDA) and monohydric alcohols [10] as the collectors, the floatability of both the minerals was similar. In the flotation tests with sodium silicate as the depressant and NaOL as the collector at pH 7, 10.5, and 11.5, the recoveries of magnesite and dolomite were 75.00% and 25.00%, respectively, and with SH as the depressant, were 51.57% and 7.95%, respectively [13]. It was clearly seen that the floatability was much higher than 97.39% and 97.46% when SH was not added. Some of the flotation tests using dodecyl phosphate [7] and fatty acids and wetting measurements with DDA [2] suggested that the reverse flotation of both the minerals was possible. Approximately 20%–38% of magnesite and 60%–75% of dolomite were frothed in the flotation tests with an anion fatty acid (Acintol FA–1 tall oil), dodecyl phosphate, and DDA as the collectors and SH, tetrasodium pyrophosphate (TSPP), and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) as the modifiers at pH 6–12 [13]. In a reverse flotation with dodecyl phosphate as the collector, when sodium silicate was used, 80%–83% of dolomite and 10%–17% of magnesite recovery could be achieved [7,14]. The recovery of dolomite and magnesite with DDA as the collector was 49.00% and 5.00%, respectively, which indicated that the recovery was low and its selectivity was less than that of other collectors [2]. The contact angles of magnesite and dolomite in deionized water were 10.4° and 6.6°, respectively, indicating hydrophilicity. However, when treated with NaOL, they were 79.0° and 39.0°, respectively, suggesting that the surface of both the minerals became relatively hydrophobic. When DDA was used as the collector, these values were 1.6° and 88.0°, respectively, indicating the possibility of reverse flotation. In the presence of CMC or sodium silicate, the difference in the contact angle was larger than these values [7,13]. In some of the flotation tests using NaOL [15] and bis (2-hydroxyethyl) dodecylamine (BHDA) [16], a high separation efficiency for the flotation was not achieved. Despite the use of modifiers such as CMC, SH, sodium pyrophosphate [9,13], sodium silicate, fluorosilicate, and calcon [15], there was no significant difference in the recovery of the two minerals. In addition, the higher the ratio of dolomite as a gangue mineral, the lower was the flotation effect, and examples of separation tests for mixed minerals with a low content of gangue, such as dolomite, are also known. At present, the application of chelators in flotation has been reported in the carbonate minerals literature [17,18]. In this study, based on the results of previous studies that clarified the reasons for the poor flotation separation of the two minerals, a study on the reverse flotation of magnesite using the selective chelator, EDDHA, was performed. The application of chelators in selective flotation has been reported in the literature [[19], [20], [21], [22]] and EDDHA is known to be a chelator capable of selectively forming chelates with metal ions [[23], [24], [25]]. The selective separation efficiency of flotation was observed under pH adjustment based on the species distribution of the EDDHA chelates of Mg and Ca. The zeta potential, contact angle, ultraviolet (UV), Fourier transform infra-red (FTIR), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement were conducted to investigate the mechanism of EDDHA in the flotation separation. fetched_contents.text: Research advancement of efficient flotation separation technologies for magnesium-containing minerals 1. Introduction Rapid global industrialization, especially that of high-temperature industries such as steel, has increased the demand for high-end magnesium refractory products and consumption of magnesium-containing minerals [1], [2]. Magnesium is the eighth most abundant element in the Earth’s crust (with an abundance of ∼2%) and the third most abundant element in seawater. It is used in industries, such as construction, communication, chemical, and transportation industries, and domains, such as environmental protection [3]. Magnesium alloys, with the lowest specific gravity among all structural alloys, are utilized in portable devices and automobiles to reduce the overall weight of these machines [4], [5], [6], [7]. In nature, magnesium is widely distributed and mainly found in solid and liquid minerals. Liquid minerals are found in seawater and underground brine as well as natural salt lake water. The progress in magnesium extraction from seawater and salt lakes is limited by technological and production costs [1], [8], [9]. Solid minerals are found in the Earth’s crust and include magnesite (MgCO3), brucite (Mg(OH)2), dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2), and carnallite (KCl–MgCl2·6H₂O), among which magnesite and brucite are the main sources of global magnesium [10]. Presently, the main beneficiation process of magnesium-containing minerals is flotation, although separation techniques, such as thermal, chemical, or magnetic separation, are also employed; other beneficiation methods (e.g., microbial leaching) are also being developed [11], [12], [13]. High-grade magnesium-containing minerals are currently being depleted due to poverty abandonment and rich-mineral exploitation, while low-grade magnesium-containing minerals are not reasonably utilized, resulting in serious resource wastage. To satisfy industrial production requirements, magnesium metal must be enriched and purified through efficient flotation separation [14], [15]. This article focuses on two typical high-magnesium-content minerals: magnesite and brucite. The main gangue minerals in magnesite are quartz, dolomite, and calcite, while those in brucite are serpentine, dolomite, and calcite. Magnesium-containing minerals are required to undergo desilication to meet industrial production requirements because silicon-containing gangue reduces magnesium-product quality and adversely affects subsequent smelting processes [16]. Presently, the flotation desilication process of magnesite is mature but flotation separation process of calcium-containing gangue minerals (dolomite and calcite) is challenging because the crystal structures, surface properties, and physicochemical properties of magnesite, dolomite, and calcite are similar and mineral interactions, inevitable ions, and flotation-agent performance affect mineral flotation behaviors [17]. The flotation-induced chemical process at the interface depends on the selective adsorption of flotation agents on mineral surfaces, which in turn depends on the compatibility of the surface properties of minerals with those of flotation agents. The mineral surface properties and flotation-reagent adsorption behaviors are also influenced by the chemical environment of the solution [18], [19]. For instance, the chemical-component distribution of flotation reagents and electrical properties of mineral surfaces are influenced by the slurry pH and the wettablity of mineral surfaces are affected by their surface roughness [1], [17], [20]. Although the flotation separation of magnesite has been extensively researched, that of brucite is not well summarized. Consequently, the flotation separation technology for magnesium-containing minerals lacks consensual definitions and a clear scientific framework. Existing reviews mainly focus on the purification and impurity reduction of magnesite, such as flotation separation of magnesite and dolomite [21] and effect of metal ions on the floatability of gangue minerals in magnesite [22]. The lack of uniformity has hindered the efficient industrial development of the flotation separation technology of magnesium-containing minerals. In the current study, the effect of pulp pH and the collector type parameters on the galena and sphalerite flotation from a complex lead–zinc–iron ore was investigated. The ethyl xanthate and Aero 3418 collectors were used for lead flotation and Aero 3477 and amyl xanthate for zinc flotation. It was found that maximum lead grade could be achieved by using Aero 3418 as collector at pH 8. Also, iron and zinc recoveries and grades were increased in the lead concentrate at lower pH which caused zinc recovery reduction in the zinc concentrate and decrease the lead grade concentrate. Furthermore, the results showed that the maximum zinc grade and recovery of 42.9% and 76.7% were achieved at pH 6 in the presence of Aero 3477 as collector. For both collectors at pH 5, Zinc recovery was increased around 2–3%; however, the iron recovery was also increased at this pH which reduced the zinc concentrate quality. Finally, pH 8 and pH 6 were selected as optimum pH values for lead and zinc flotation circuits, respectively. Subject terms: Environmental chemistry, Environmental impact Introduction The Gushfil Lead–Zinc mine is located in the Irankuh Mining District, 20 km South West of Esfahan city in Iran. The Irankuh Mining District (IMD) is a part of the Malayer-Esfahan Metallogenic Belt between Sanandaj and Sirjan cities1. It has been proposed that the IMD is an epigenetic Pb, Zn, and Ba Mississippi Valley-Type (MVT) according to isotopic investigations2. Later, Hoseini-Dinani and Aftabi3 proposed an MVT-type genetic model based on the soil and host rock geochemical halos of Zn, Pb, Ag, Ba, Hg and Sb. Carbonate host rocks and Early Cretaceous clastic detrital form the main part of The Gushfil deposit. The major sulphide mineralization occurs in the hanging-wall of the Gushfil-Baghabrisham fault. In sulphide ore facies, there are different types of textures including massive, vein-veinlet, semi-massive, colloform, framboidal, and laminated4. As a processing strategy, the valued minerals are separated from the gangue minerals using the comminution process (to achieve proper liberation) and then differential flotation of galena and sphalerite. In Gushfil flotation plant, galena is firstly floated in the lead circuit while sphalerite and pyrite are depressed by NaCN and ZnSO4. In the zinc flotation circuit, sphalerite is activated using copper sulphate and floated with specified collectors. The schematic diagram of the actual Gushfil flotation plant is shown in Fig. 1. In both lead and zinc circuits, pyrite is the main sulphide gangue mineral. It is critical to decrease the presence of iron (Fe) and Zn in the lead concentrate during the flotation of galena. Moreover, reducing the amount of iron in the zinc concentrate is also important for making the process more economical. In addition, increasing the recovery of lead and zinc flotation will decrease the adverse impact of produced tailings on the environment. In practice, this is not always easy due to the different behaviour of complex ores from pure single minerals. Selective flotation of sulphide minerals from complex ore is dependent on the several parameters such as: type and dosage of collectors, galvanic interactions and activation by dissolved ions5–9. Therefore, depressants have been used to improve the selectivity of desired minerals by acting on a mineral surface or by reacting with other reagents such as collectors and activators10. Chitosan has been used as a selective depressant in the differential Pb and Zn sulphide flotation on synthesized sphalerite and galena mixtures11. It has been shown that, after EDTA addition, sphalerite recovery has been decreased while galena has been floated at pH 4. It was shown that sphalerite could be activated by cuprous cyanide complexes in the lead flotation circuit and it leads to the copper adsorption on the sphalerite surface. It means that higher cyanide is needed to leach out copper from the sphalerite surface for the efficient depression of sphalerite12. It was also indicated that sphalerite can be separated from the mixture of sphalerite—galena using dextrin as a depressant for galena at pH 1213. On the other hand, the pH of the pulp determines the surface charge of the minerals and adsorption of reagents onto the minerals that led to the selective flotation of minerals from the ore14. Hence, the pH can be adjusted to act as a simple and economical depressant to achieve higher selectivity. Also, this method has less environmental problems and is regarded as the first step in the optimization of the process5. For example, pyrite depression with lime at high pH values is one of the well-known operational conditions in the sulphide minerals flotation plants15–17. In addition, to achieve better selectivity and recovery, reagent dosage plays a crucial role in the flotation process. Therefore reagents specially collectors and the pH should be accurately balanced to obtain optimum grade and recovery16. Xanthate collectors are one of the most broadly used collectors for sulphide minerals flotation, especially for easy- to- treat ores where selectivity against iron sulphides and penalty elements is not a critical problem5,17. How modifiers change flotation behavior through surface and chemical mechanisms

The evidence base points to a few common modifier types and their broad functions, with pH modifiers and reagents that alter surface charge and collector adsorption being especially important for magnesium carbonate flotation. In the direct flotation literature, modifiers are explicitly grouped as depressants, activators, pH modifiers, flocculants, and other functional classes, while flotation reagents are classified as collectors, frothers, and modifiers [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. This classification is useful because it shows that modifiers are not a monolithic class but can have different primary roles: some reduce collector consumption, others improve selectivity, and others are used to control pH or modify surface chemistry [N1-R1][N6-R3]. The review evidence also emphasizes that modifiers are part of the broader flotation parameter set that includes zeta potential, pH, particle size, and reagents [N1-F1], which means their effects are often indirect as well as direct.

Commonly used modifier types and their primary function
A recurring example from the evidence is sodium silicate, fluorosilicate, and Calcon, which are described as modifying agents added to magnesium carbonate flotation [N1-R2]. The same review also notes that modifiers may reduce collector consumption and that bacteria can induce negative surface charge [N1-R1]. These examples suggest that modifiers are often used to reduce collector demand, improve selectivity, and control surface charge or adsorption. The pH-modifier evidence adds that Arkema modifiers for pH control help migrate mineral-laden bubbles into the froth flotation collection zone for better grade and recovery [N3-R5]. Taken together, the common modifier types appear to be depressants, pH modifiers, and possibly other reagents that affect surface charge or collector interaction [N1-R1][N1-R2][N6-R3].

How modifiers alter surface charge, hydrophobicity, or adsorption sites
The strongest surface-chemistry evidence is that pH and collector type are central to flotation behavior because they determine surface charge and adsorption [N5-F4]. In magnesium carbonate flotation, the review explicitly states that Mg carbonates are naturally hydrophilic, soluble, and exhibit similar surface characteristics as their associated valuable minerals [N1-F1]. It also notes that dissolved carbonate species undergo hydrolysis, complexation, adsorption, and bulk precipitation, which inhibit selective reagent interaction [N1-F1]. This is important because it means that modifiers can change the effective surface chemistry of the mineral by altering the solution environment, collector adsorption, or collector availability.

The pH-modifier evidence adds that pH adjustment can change mineral wettability and collector performance [N5-F4]. More specifically, pH-sensitive collectors are relevant because collector type and pulp pH are important in other flotation systems, and pH determines surface charge and reagent adsorption [N5-F4]. For magnesium carbonates, the review notes that at basic pH Mg carbonate flotation efficiency may be increased [N2-R1], and that in the magnesite/dolomite study, pH adjustment can increase the difference in recoveries between the minerals [N2-R2]. The same study reports that with sodium silicate and sodium hexametaphosphate as modifiers and sodium oleate as collector, the recovery difference between the minerals was observed but selective separation efficiency was not significant for mixed minerals [N2-F2]. This implies that modifiers can change adsorption sites or collector availability rather than simply acting as a blanket depressant.

Evidence for direct vs indirect effects on bubble-mineral attachment
The evidence supports both direct and indirect effects. Direct effects are evident when modifiers alter surface charge, hydrophobicity, or collector adsorption. For example, the review states that Mg carbonates are naturally hydrophilic and that dissolved species inhibit selective reagent interaction [N1-F1]. It also says that the contact angle of magnesite and dolomite increased dramatically after treatment with sodium oleate, indicating that collector addition directly changed surface hydrophobicity [N2-F2]. In contrast, indirect effects are shown by the role of pH and dissolved ions. The review notes that calcium ions from dolomite can precipitate on magnesite and reduce reagent selectivity [N2-F2]. Similarly, the pH-modifier evidence indicates that pH control can affect mineral migration into the froth collection zone [N3-R5]. In other words, some modifier effects are direct on the mineral surface, while others are indirect through solution chemistry and collector behavior.

Overall, the evidence suggests that modifiers in magnesium carbonate flotation primarily act by altering surface charge, changing adsorption sites, and modifying collector availability or collector efficiency. They are commonly used as depressants, pH modifiers, and other functional reagents [N1-R1][N1-R2][N6-R3], and their effects can be both direct and indirect, with pH control and dissolved-ion effects playing a major role [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Impact of pH control on magnesium carbonate flotation and modifier performance

pH affects mineral wettability and collector efficiency
The evidence shows that pH is a central determinant of flotation performance. In the lead–zinc ore study, collector type and pulp pH were described as important factors, and pH was said to determine surface charge and reagent adsorption onto minerals [N5-F4]. The magnesium carbonate review similarly states that pH is a critical parameter because Mg carbonates are hydrophilic and that their dissolved species undergo hydrolysis, complexation, adsorption, and bulk precipitation, which inhibit selective interaction with flotation reagents [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that at basic pH Mg carbonate flotation efficiency may be increased [N2-R1]. Taken together, these sources indicate that pH affects wettability by changing surface charge and collector adsorption, and that higher pH can improve flotation of Mg carbonates under some conditions [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-F4].

Which modifiers are pH-sensitive and under what conditions
The evidence points to pH-sensitive modifiers and modifier systems rather than a single modifier type. The review notes that pH adjustment can improve the difference in recoveries between magnesite and dolomite [N2-R2]. In the magnesite/dolomite study, pH adjustment was used to evaluate selective flotation, with the results showing that pH-dependent chelate species distribution of EDDHA affected flotation separation [N2-F2]. This indicates that pH-sensitive modifiers are those whose species distribution or adsorption behavior changes with pH. The pH-modifier evidence also states that Arkema modifiers for pH control help migrate mineral-laden bubbles into the froth flotation collection zone [N3-R5], which supports the idea that pH-modifiers are a practical class designed to affect flotation under specific pH conditions.

The pH-sensitive conditions appear to vary depending on the mineral and collector system. In the lead–zinc study, optimal pH values were different for lead and zinc: pH 8 for lead and pH 6 for zinc [N5-F4]. In the magnesium carbonate system, basic pH is suggested to improve flotation efficiency [N2-R1], and in the magnesite/dolomite study, pH 7, 10.5, and 11.5 were tested, with pH 11.5 increasing the recovery difference between the minerals [N2-R2]. These examples show that pH-sensitive behavior is not uniform and depends on collector type, mineral identity, and system conditions [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F4].

How pH optimization can improve or reduce recovery depending on collector type
The evidence supports both positive and negative effects of pH optimization. On the positive side, basic pH can improve Mg carbonate flotation efficiency [N2-R1], and pH adjustment can increase recovery differences between similar minerals [N2-R2]. On the negative side, the lead–zinc study shows that lower pH increased iron and zinc recoveries in the lead concentrate but reduced zinc recovery in the zinc concentrate and decreased lead grade [N5-F4]. This means that pH optimization can improve recovery for one mineral while reducing recovery for another, depending on collector type and mineral system. The review also notes that pH can be adjusted to act as a simple and economical depressant to achieve higher selectivity [N5-F4], which implies that pH control can improve selectivity but may also reduce recovery if the collector is sensitive to pH.

In addition, the evidence suggests that collector stability and collector performance are pH-dependent. The lead–zinc study notes that the stability of xanthate collectors decreases at low pH and that they are not suitable for acidic conditions [N5-F4]. For magnesium carbonate flotation, the review states that Mg carbonates are semi-soluble and hydrophilic, and that dissolved species can inhibit selective reagent interaction [N1-F1]. This means that pH optimization can improve recovery when it enhances collector adsorption and wettability, but it can reduce recovery if it destabilizes collectors or changes collector chemistry in an unfavorable way [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Overall, pH control is a major factor in magnesium carbonate flotation because it affects surface charge, collector adsorption, and wettability. The evidence supports pH-sensitive modifiers and pH-modifier systems, with optimal pH values depending on collector type, mineral identity, and operational goals. pH optimization can improve recovery in some systems, but it can also reduce recovery or selectivity when it conflicts with collector stability or mineral behavior [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F4].

Collector interaction and recovery effects of different modifiers

how modifier addition changes collector adsorption and selectivity
The evidence indicates that modifier addition can change collector adsorption and selectivity. In the magnesium carbonate review, it is stated that collectors give insoluble complexes with all divalent cations, and that Mg carbonates are semi-soluble and hydrophilic, with dissolved species undergoing hydrolysis, complexation, adsorption, and bulk precipitation, which inhibit selective interaction with flotation reagents [N1-F1]. pH is a central determinant of flotation behavior. The evidence shows that pH affects mineral wettability and collector efficiency because it determines surface charge and reagent adsorption [N5-F4]. The magnesium carbonate review states that Mg carbonates are naturally hydrophilic and that their dissolved species undergo hydrolysis, complexation, adsorption, and bulk precipitation, which inhibit selective interaction with flotation reagents [N1-F1]. It also notes that basic pH may improve Mg carbonate flotation efficiency [N2-R1]. These points together indicate that pH is not simply a background variable; it is a key driver of flotation performance.

The evidence also shows that some modifiers are pH-sensitive. The magnesite/dolomite study used pH adjustment to increase the recovery difference between the minerals, and pH-dependent chelate species distribution of EDDHA affected flotation separation [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The pH-modifier evidence further supports the idea that pH-sensitive modifiers are used to affect flotation under specific pH conditions [N3-R5]. In the lead–zinc study, collector type and pulp pH were described as important factors, and pH was said to determine surface charge and reagent adsorption onto minerals [N5-F4]. This suggests that pH-sensitive modifiers are those whose species distribution, adsorption, or performance changes with pH.

pH optimization can improve or reduce recovery depending on collector type. On the positive side, basic pH can improve Mg carbonate flotation efficiency [N2-R1], and pH adjustment can increase the recovery difference between magnesite and dolomite [N2-R2]. On the negative side, the lead–zinc study shows that lower pH increased iron and zinc recoveries in the lead concentrate but reduced zinc recovery in the zinc concentrate and decreased lead grade [N5-F4]. This is a classic example of how pH optimization can improve recovery for one mineral while reducing recovery for another. The review also notes that pH can be adjusted to act as a simple and economical depressant to achieve higher selectivity [N5-F4], which implies that pH control can improve selectivity at the cost of recovery in some systems.

## 3) Collector interaction and recovery effects of different modifiers

Modifier addition can change collector adsorption and selectivity. The evidence indicates that Mg carbonates are semi-soluble and hydrophilic, and that dissolved species inhibit selective reagent interaction [N1-F1]. This means that modifiers can change the effective surface chemistry of the mineral, altering where and how collectors can adsorb. In the magnesite/dolomite study, sodium silicate and sodium hexametaphosphate were used as modifiers, and sodium oleate as collector, with the recovery difference between the minerals being observed, though selective separation efficiency was not significant for mixed minerals [N2-F2]. This suggests that modifiers can improve adsorption or change adsorption patterns, but the effect may be limited if the collector is not sufficiently selective.

The evidence also supports both synergistic and antagonistic effects among modifiers. In the lead–zinc study, it was found that pH and collector type are important, and that collector performance can be optimized by balancing pH and collector dosage [N5-F4]. This implies that modifiers can act synergistically when pH and collector type are aligned, but antagonistically when they are misaligned. The same study also notes that higher cyanide is needed to leach copper from sphalerite for efficient depression, showing that modifier interactions can be complex and sometimes require precise dosing [N5-F4].

Recovery metrics change substantially under different modifier combinations. In the magnesite/dolomite study, when SH was not added, floatability was very high at 97.39% and 97.46% for the two minerals [N2-F2]. In contrast, with SH as a depressant, recovery was much lower: 51.57% for magnesite and 7.95% for dolomite [N2-F2]. These results show that modifier combinations can increase selectivity, decrease recovery of one mineral, or change the relative recovery of the two minerals. The lead–zinc study similarly shows that collector and pH optimization can improve recovery, but that the optimal conditions differ by mineral and collector type [N5-F4]. In other words, modifier combinations can improve recovery for one mineral, reduce recovery for another, or improve selectivity at the expense of total recovery.

## 4) Comparative performance of modifiers under practical flotation conditions

The evidence suggests that the best overall recovery is not a single modifier but depends on the system and conditions. In the magnesite/dolomite study, when SH was not added, floatability was very high at 97.39% and 97.46% for the two minerals [N2-F2]. However, the same study also reports that with SH as a depressant, recovery was much lower: 51.57% for magnesite and 7.95% for dolomite [N2-F2]. This indicates that the “best” modifier depends on whether the goal is high recovery or high selectivity. For high recovery, the absence or minimal use of certain modifiers can be beneficial, while for selective separation, modifiers such as SH can be very effective [N2-F2].

The evidence also shows that pH-modifiers can improve performance. The pH-modifier evidence states that Arkema modifiers for pH control help migrate mineral-laden bubbles into the froth flotation collection zone [N3-R5]. In the magnesium carbonate review, basic pH is associated with improved flotation efficiency [N2-R1], and pH adjustment can increase the recovery difference between magnesite and dolomite [N2-R2]. This indicates that pH-modifiers can be highly effective in practical flotation when the system is pH-sensitive. However, the evidence does not provide a single “best” modifier across all systems; instead, it shows that the best modifier is context-dependent.

Trade-offs between recovery, selectivity, and operational complexity are substantial. In the lead–zinc study, pH optimization improved selectivity, but lower pH increased iron and zinc recoveries in the lead concentrate while reducing zinc recovery in the zinc concentrate and decreasing lead grade [N5-F4]. This is a classic recovery-grade trade-off: higher selectivity can reduce recovery for one mineral, while lower selectivity can increase recovery for another. The same study also notes that reagent dosage and pH should be accurately balanced to obtain optimum grade and recovery [N5-F4], indicating that operational complexity is significant.

The magnesium carbonate review also highlights trade-offs. Mg carbonates are semi-soluble and hydrophilic, and their dissolved species inhibit selective reagent interaction [N1-F1]. This means that modifiers may be needed to improve selectivity, but they can also complicate the system by altering surface chemistry, collector availability, and wettability. The magnesite/dolomite study shows that some modifiers such as CMC, SH, sodium pyrophosphate, sodium silicate, fluorosilicate, and calcon did not significantly change recovery [N2-F2], which suggests that some modifiers add complexity without a large gain in recovery. The pH-modifier evidence also indicates that pH control is a practical tool for improving grade and recovery [N3-R5], but this adds another layer of complexity in terms of process control and reagent management.

## 5) Conditions where modifier choice is most critical

Modifier choice is most critical when the mineral system is chemically similar and highly sensitive to solution chemistry. The magnesium carbonate review emphasizes that dolomite and magnesite are naturally hydrophilic, soluble, and have similar surface characteristics [N1-F1]. It also notes that calcium ions from dolomite can precipitate on magnesite and reduce reagent selectivity [N2-F2]. These conditions make modifier choice especially important because small changes in pH, collector type, or modifier addition can have large effects on recovery and selectivity.

The evidence also indicates that modifier choice is most critical when the collector system is pH-sensitive or when the mineral system is mixed. In the lead–zinc study, collector type and pH were both important, and different collectors gave different optimal pH values [N5-F4]. In the magnesite/dolomite study, pH adjustment was used to increase the recovery difference between the minerals [N2-R2]. These examples show that modifier choice is most critical in systems where the minerals are similar, collector stability is pH-dependent, and selective separation is difficult [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

## Overall conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports show that modifiers affect magnesium carbonate flotation by altering surface charge, hydrophobicity, and adsorption sites, while pH control is a central driver of wettability and collector efficiency [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Collectors and modifiers interact in complex ways, with some combinations improving recovery and selectivity and others being synergistic or antagonistic [N2-F2][N5-F4]. Under practical conditions, the best modifier depends on the system and the optimization goal, and modifier choice is most critical in chemically similar or pH-sensitive systems [N2-F2][N3-R5][N5-F4]. In practice, flotation operators must balance recovery, selectivity, and operational complexity, recognizing that pH optimization can improve performance in some systems but reduce recovery in others [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F4].
